extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of logic and philosophy; logicians and philosophers studying the nature and import of propositions
extracted.subtask_description: Classification and analysis of names, predicates, and propositions: forms (affirmative/negative, simple/compound, hypothetical/categorical), quantificational scope (universal/particular/indefinite/singular), the function of the copula, and the import of propositions as statements about things rather than merely about ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of Namable Things
rubrics_metrics.description: An enumeration and classification of all Namable Things into four classes: 1st. Feelings, or States of Consciousness. 2d. The Minds which experience those feelings. 3d. The Bodies, or external objects which excite certain of those feelings, together with the powers or properties whereby they excite them. 4th. The Successions and Co-existences, the Likenesses and Unlikenesses, between feelings or states of consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four classes (feelings, minds, bodies, and relations among feelings) are proposed as a substitute for Aristotle's Categories. Practical application follows in analysing the import of propositions: whatever a name signifies must be composed of some of these classes. Objective facts are grounded on corresponding subjective facts; attributes and relations ultimately trace to sensations or states of consciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of Feelings (fundamental namables)
rubrics_metrics.description: Feelings are of four sorts: Sensations, Thoughts, Emotions, and Volitions. Perceptions are a particular case of Belief, and Belief is a kind of thought. Actions are merely volitions followed by an effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing what a name or proposition refers to, determine which sort of feeling (sensation, thought, emotion, volition) is involved. This taxonomy underpins later distinctions between psychological (subjective) and objective facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substances: Bodies vs Minds (epistemic grounding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Substances are either Bodies or Minds. All we can know of Matter is the sensations it gives us and the order of occurrence of those sensations; the substance Body is the unknown cause of our sensations, and the substance Mind is the unknown recipient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the epistemic limits: when propositions refer to 'bodies' we only have access to the sensations and their order; treat 'body' and 'mind' as theoretical placeholders for causes/recipients beyond immediate consciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attributes grounded in states of consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Attributes are of three kinds—Quality, Relation, and Quantity—and are known only by the sensations or other states of consciousness they excite. Qualities, relations (except the simplest), and quantities are grounded on some fact or phenomenon (series of sensations or states of consciousness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In predication one is really referring to sensations or states of consciousness. Examples: the beauty of a statue is grounded on the pleasure the statue produces (an emotion), and quantity is grounded on discernible differences in sensation (bulk, intensity). This cautions against reifying attributes beyond their experiential basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascribing attributes to minds: internal state vs effect on others
rubrics_metrics.description: An attribute of a mind consists either in being itself affected in a certain way, or affecting other minds in a certain way. Many ascriptions (especially terms of praise or blame) are twofold: they assert a habitual state of the person's sentient existence and that contemplation of that state excites approbation or blame in others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When attributing character terms (e.g., 'devout', 'generous', 'admirable'), distinguish (a) the subject's recurring internal feelings/volitions and (b) the secondary feelings those states produce in observers (approval, admiration). Example: 'generosity' implies both a state in the agent and that the idea of that state excites approbation in others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition defined: predicate affirmed or denied of a subject; role of the copula
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposition is a portion of discourse in which a predicate is affirmed or denied of a subject. The sign that distinguishes predication is commonly the copula (forms of the verb 'to be' such as 'is' or 'is not'), or sometimes inflection. The copula is the sign of predication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure a clear understanding of the copula's office: it marks that one term is being affirmed or denied of another. Lack of clarity about the copula's role leads to metaphysical confusions. When analysing sentences, identify the copula to see whether a predication is intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conflating the copula with existence ('is' ambiguity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The copula is only a sign of predication and does not necessarily signify existence. The ambiguity of 'is' (to be as copula vs to exist) has caused many philosophical errors; for example, 'A centaur is a fiction of the poets' does not imply a centaur exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not read existential claims into every occurrence of 'is'. Distinguish uses of 'is' as copula (predication) from uses asserting existence; treat such ambiguity as a source of metaphysical fog and avoid building theories on it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affirmative vs Negative propositions (and limits of treating negation as a negative name)
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions divide into affirmative (predicate affirmed of subject) and negative (predicate denied). Some logicians reduce negation by making the predicate a negative name ('not dead'), but this treats absence as a positive predicate and confuses the real distinction between a fact and the non-existence of that fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize negation as a distinct logical operation (denial) rather than merely affirmation of a negative name; be wary of 'verbal simplifications' that obscure the factual difference between presence and absence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tense and modality attach to the copula (predication), not to the predicate
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences of tense (past, present, future) are properly designations belonging to the event asserted and attach to the copula—the sign of predication—rather than to the predicate itself. Modal words like 'may', 'perhaps', 'possible' often express the state of our mind (absence of disbelief) rather than properties of the fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing modal or temporal statements, treat time and modality as attributes of the predication (the copula) and be alert that some modals express epistemic stance rather than metaphysical modality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple vs Compound (Complex) propositions; conjunctions as abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: A simple proposition affirms or denies one predicate of one subject. What are called compound propositions often are merely multiple propositions joined by conjunctions; words like 'and' or 'but' are syncategorematic abbreviations (they add a further proposition, e.g., of contrast).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When parsing purportedly 'compound' sentences, check whether they are truly a single assertion or several distinct assertions linked by particles. Expand syncategorematic particles into the propositions they abbreviate to avoid conflating separate assertions into one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothetical (Conditional) and Disjunctive propositions as propositions about propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypothetical (conditional) propositions are propositions concerning propositions: their subject and predicate are themselves names of propositions (e.g., 'If A is B, C is D' asserts that 'C is D' is a legitimate inference from 'A is B'). Disjunctive propositions ('Either A is B or C is D') are resolvable into conditionals and are therefore conditional in meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat hypotheticals as assertions about inferential relations (inferribility) rather than as ordinary predications of things. Recognize disjunctions can be analysed into conditional forms; do not conflate the embedded simple propositions with the single assertion the conditional/hypothetical makes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categorical (non-conditional) propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Categorical propositions are those in which the assertion is not dependent on a condition; they assert directly of the subject something that is not framed as an inference from another proposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish categorical from hypothetical forms: categorical assertions predicate of things directly, whereas hypotheticals predicate inferability relations between propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantificational scope: Universal, Particular, Indefinite, and Singular propositions; Distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions differ by the degree of generality of the subject: Universal (All men are mortal), Particular (Some men are mortal), Indefinite (form not showing whether universal or particular), and Singular (subject an individual). A term is 'distributed' when it stands for each and every individual it denotes. A universal proposition is one in which the subject is distributed; a particular proposition is one in which the subject is undistributed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the subject term is intended universally or particularly (consider context and ordinary usage where indicators may be omitted). Use the notion of distribution to analyse syllogistic relations (e.g., in 'All men are mortal' the subject 'man' is distributed; in 'Some men are mortal' it is not). Beware 'indefinite' formulations and seek contextual cues to resolve them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Import of propositions: propositions concern things, not merely ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposition's immediate object is what is believed about the things themselves, not about our ideas. The common tradition treating propositions as relations between ideas (the act of judgment as putting ideas together) mistakes the matter: propositions (except when explicitly about ideas) assert facts about external phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing or evaluating propositions, focus on what they assert about external facts or phenomena rather than construing them primarily as mental operations on ideas. Recognize that mental processes (ideas) are necessary conditions for belief but are not the proper object of the proposition unless explicitly so stated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hobbes' account: truth as predicational name-identity (diagnostic remark)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hobbes' view: in every proposition what is signified is the speaker's belief that the predicate is a name of the same thing of which the subject is a name; if it really is so, the proposition is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This account captures a necessary property of true propositions (subject and predicate must be names of the same thing when true), but it is presented as one theory among others; use it diagnostically to check whether a given predication aligns in reference between subject and predicate.
